tier_reason: The bench page (opened as the quickjs-zh translated mirror bench.md; the bellard.org original is EGRESS_BLOCKED, a search snippet of an HN comment links it and repeats the same totals) runs the public V8 benchmark suite version 7 (bench-v8; harness invoked by the bellard/quickjs Makefile target `bench-v8`: `make -C tests/bench-v8; ./qjs -d tests/bench-v8/combined.js`) on QuickJS and Duktape 2.3.0, both built with gcc 4.9.2 -O2 on Fedora 21, on a Core i5 4570 at 3.2 GHz. Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated, so A holds.

corrections.caveats: Numbers are from 2019 (QuickJS 2019-07-09, Duktape 2.3.0, gcc 4.9.2) and were run by QuickJS's own author. The page opened is a Chinese-language mirror of the author's bench page (quickjs-zh/QuickJS bench.md); the original bellard.org/quickjs/bench.html is blocked here and was not opened, though a search snippet confirms the same 942 vs 408 totals. The bench-v8 directory the Makefile target uses is absent from the GitHub tree at HEAD and from an unpacked-tarball mirror (twardoch/quickjs-1); it is distributed separately on bellard.org (not verified here), while the underlying V8 v7 suite is public (e.g. mozilla arewefastyet v8-v7). Independent corroboration on current versions: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark CI (10/5/2026) scores QuickJS 2026.06.04 at 1217 vs Duktape 489 on ubuntu, 1761 vs 905 on macos-arm64 and 1067 vs 371 on windows (about 2.5x, 1.9x and 2.9x, derived from page data). QuickJS is itself one of the category's named baselines, and it is an interpreter: JIT engines (V8, JavaScriptCore, ChakraCore) are 15-40x faster on the same suite.

notes: Numbers match the mirror page row for row (Total 942 vs 408, every sub-test as quoted). Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 11k stars, last commit 2026-09-29, not archived. Shortcoming to record: harness directory not in the public GitHub tree, original page only via mirror, 2019 numbers by the author.

tier_reason: Independent third-party shootout (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark) with public harness code (v8-v7/, forked from mozilla arewefastyet) runs ChakraCore, QuickJS and Duktape on GitHub-hosted CI runners; CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated, so it falls short of A. The suite is small (59 stars), but it is independent of ChakraCore, which keeps it at B under the independent-measurement rule.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. The ubuntu binary comes from ahaoboy/ChakraCore-build build.sh, which clones ChakraCore at HEAD (depth 1), runs ChakraCore's default ./build.sh and copies out/Release/ch (Release build; compiler and flags not stated). The windows column is version 1.11.24.0, provenance not checked.
corrections.caveats: Third-party shootout run by CI on GitHub-hosted runners (results dated 10/5/2026); CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated and engine binaries come from per-engine build repos (ahaoboy/ChakraCore-build, 0 stars), so this is tier B rather than A. The suite is a small independent project (59 stars). It compares a JIT engine against interpreters: ChakraCore's win over QuickJS (19392 vs 1217 ubuntu, 27267 vs 1067 windows) and Duktape (19392 vs 489 ubuntu) is the JIT-vs-interpreter gap, and it costs size (19.3M total vs 1M for QuickJS on ubuntu). Among embeddable JIT engines it is not the fastest: V8 scores 48107 on ubuntu (about 2.5x ChakraCore, derived from page data), and ChakraCore is not built for macOS arm64 in this suite. Community-maintained since Microsoft ended support of 1.11 on 2021-03-09; commits are sparse (latest 2026-02-19). Different versions per OS (1.13.0.0.beta on ubuntu, 1.11.24.0 on windows).

notes: Numbers are in ChakraCore's own column of the shared table on all three listed rows (ubuntu Score 19392, windows Score 27267; QuickJS 1217 and 1067). Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 9.3k stars, last commit 2026-02-19, not archived. Shortcoming to record: JIT-vs-interpreter comparison, slower than V8 by about 2.5x, large binary, unstated CPU and flags.

tier_reason: Independent third-party shootout (r-lyeh scriptorium, 525 stars, archived) with public harness (bench.cc, run.bat, tests/fib.scm and tests/fib.lua) shows chibi 1.009 s vs Lua 1.341 s; compiler is only 'VS2015 RC if possible, VS2013 elsewhere', flags are unstated and the CPU is given as 'AMD A10 3.8 GHz' without a model number, so not A.

corrections.workload: Scriptorium: recursive Fibonacci fib(34) as a top-level/global function in each language, whole-process wall time (startup included) averaged over 5 runs via system() in bench.cc; seconds, lower is better.
corrections.caveats: Marginal win (about 1.3x) on one recursive-Fibonacci micro-benchmark from July 2015 on Windows 7; the page says to take it with a grain of salt. Versions per the scriptorium tree: chibi-scheme 0.7.3 (scheme/chibi-scheme/VERSION) against PUC Lua 5.3.1 (lua/lua-5.3.1); current Lua 5.4 and current chibi were not measured. Timing is whole-process wall time including interpreter startup, build flags are not stated and the CPU model is not given. LuaJIT (0.111 s) and LuaJIT with the JIT off (0.521 s) are both faster than chibi on the same page.

notes: Row 10 (chibi 1.009 s, x01.3) and row 12 (lua 1.341 s) match the claim; both fib scripts compute fib(34) with a global recursive function, so the comparison is like for like. Metadata checked on github.com: COPYING is BSD-3-Clause text, 1.4k stars, last commit 2026-09-27. Shortcoming to record: single 2015 micro-benchmark, marginal win over an old Lua 5.3.1, slower than LuaJIT.
